column4: The ayah gathers all three movements developed in the section: the Prophet's face turns repeatedly toward heaven, God turns him to a qiblah he will be pleased with, and commands فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ toward it.
The ayah joins guidance, spending, and the exact motive إِلَّا ٱبْتِغَآءَ وَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ, closely reproducing the section's movement from God's guidance to giving solely in search of His face.
Those who persevere ٱبْتِغَآءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِمْ and spend secretly and openly enact the section's effortful face-seeking through sustained action and giving.
The feeders say their gift is only لِوَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ and seek neither repayment nor thanks, the closest parallel to 92:19-20's unrecompensed gift and sought face.
The ayah contrasts an outlay intended to grow through people's wealth with zakat given تُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ ٱللَّهِ; the sought face determines whether giving is self-returning or Godward.
Giving the relative, needy person, and traveler their due is identified as good for those يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ ٱللَّهِ, making concrete the section's giving as a direction toward God's face.
Those who call on their Lord morning and evening يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ keep their attention fixed on the sought face across the day's recurring turns.
The Prophet is told to keep with those who call on their Lord morning and evening يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ and not let his eyes pass beyond them, explicitly combining face-seeking with disciplined gaze.
Those who spend their wealth ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ unite strenuous seeking, giving, and God's pleasure, the same sequence that runs from 92:18 through 92:21.
A person sells his very self ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ, so the search for divine pleasure takes the whole person rather than only the face as a bodily part.
Moses says وَعَجِلْتُ إِلَيْكَ رَبِّ لِتَرْضَىٰ: his people are on his track, he hastens directly toward his Lord, and the movement ends in sought pleasure.
وَلَسَوْفَ يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرْضَىٰ closely echoes 92:21's promise in wording and cadence while making the Lord's giving the cause of the promised satisfaction.
The believers seek God's bounty and pleasure while the mark of prostration is on their faces; sought approval, bodily orientation, and face are visibly joined in one ayah.
فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا۟ فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ ٱللَّهِ makes every act of turning a possible orientation toward God's face, precisely joining the two key word-images.
وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ states that the Lord's face remains, grounding the section's identification of the face with God Himself and the lasting object of the search.
كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ makes God's face the sole exception to universal perishing, clarifying why seeking that face gives the search an enduring end.
Abraham declares إِنِّى وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِىَ toward the Creator of the heavens and earth, an exact Quranic enactment of the section's idiom “I turned my face to God.”
مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُۥ لِلَّهِ uses the face for the surrendered self and promises security from fear and grief, illustrating the section's “face as person” sense.
“I have surrendered my face to God” is followed in the same ayah by فَإِن تَوَلَّوْا۟: submission turns the whole self toward God, while refusal turns away from the message.
The best religion is attributed to one who أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُۥ لِلَّهِ while doing good, again making face both the self and its Godward orientation.
Whoever يُسْلِمْ وَجْهَهُۥٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ has grasped the firm handhold, and the ayah ends with all outcomes returning to God; direction and destination coincide.
The command أَقِيمُوا۟ وُجُوهَكُمْ عِندَ كُلِّ مَسْجِدٍ and sincere invocation turns the face bodily and the religion inwardly toward the same addressee.
The imperative أَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ حَنِيفًا commands a settled face-direction, the positive end of the section's two-sided turning.
فَأَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ حَنِيفًا repeats the command to set one's face firmly toward the upright religion and associates that orientation with God's created pattern.
The repeated command أَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ ٱلْقَيِّمِ adds urgency: establish the face's direction before a day that cannot be turned back.
The qiblah passage opens with the question مَا وَلَّىٰهُمْ عَن قِبْلَتِهِمُ: what turned them away from their former direction, preparing the commanded turn of 2:144.
وَلِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا gives each community a direction toward which it turns and immediately commands a race in good deeds, joining orientation with energetic pursuit.
The repeated command فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ makes the bodily face carry an obedient direction beyond the first command in 2:144.
The qiblah command is extended to the Prophet and community wherever they are, so many faces share the same deliberate direction.

Moses vows not to cease moving until he reaches the junction of the two seas even if he travels for ages, a direct Quranic scene of the section's seeker who will not stand still or abandon the search.
At the sought junction Moses and his companion lose notice of their fish as it takes a path into the sea, supplying the missing-object event that drives the search scene through 18:64.
The companion recalls the forgotten fish and its strange path into the sea, identifying the lost sign and the place to which the seekers must return.
Moses says ذَٰلِكَ مَا كُنَّا نَبْغِ and they return عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَارِهِمَا قَصَصًا; what they sought is recovered by turning back and following their own tracks.
Jacob orders his sons to go and search carefully for Joseph and his brother and not despair, a sustained search for lost loved ones whose hope keeps it moving.
إِنَّكَ كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا فَمُلَاقِيهِ turns a lifetime of strenuous movement toward the Lord into an eventual meeting, matching the section's search ending face to face.
وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاضِرَةٌ places radiant faces at the opening of the encounter completed in 75:23.
إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ gives those faces a single object of gaze—their Lord—making literal the section's image of a face kept toward what it seeks.
ٱرْجِعِىٓ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً مَّرْضِيَّةً combines return toward the Lord with being pleased and pleasing, a compact version of directed movement ending in mutual acceptance.
وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَّاعِمَةٌ introduces blessed faces whose inward result is specified by their satisfaction in the next ayah.
لِّسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ makes the faces of 88:8 satisfied with their striving, bringing face, effort, and رضى together as the section does.
The warning that punishment is upon مَن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ exactly repeats the section's paired denial and turning away.
وَلَٰكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ repeats the exact pair and makes bodily departure from the truth the culmination of the refusal described in 75:31.
أَرَءَيْتَ إِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ applies the exact denial-and-turning pair to the man who tries to stop a servant from praying.
Believers are commanded to obey God and His messenger and not تَوَلَّوْا۟ عَنْهُ while they hear, directly defining turning away as failure to heed rather than merely bodily motion.
The warning not to resemble people who say “we hear” while they do not hear spells out the refused listening implicit in the turning of 8:20.
Even if God made the unresponsive hear, لَتَوَلَّوا۟ وَّهُم مُّعْرِضُونَ; hearing followed by deliberate aversion exactly illustrates the section's nonbodily sense of tawallī.
A group says it believes and obeys, then يَتَوَلَّىٰ after that; the change exposes turning away as abandonment of professed obedience.
The believers' answer سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا supplies the exact opposite of the refused hearing and obedience staged in 24:47-48.
فَمَا لَهُمْ عَنِ ٱلتَّذْكِرَةِ مُعْرِضِينَ names the people's aversion from the reminder before the next two ayat render that aversion as animal flight.
كَأَنَّهُمْ حُمُرٌ مُّسْتَنفِرَةٌ turns the avoiders into startled wild donkeys, a close Quranic counterpart to the section's dictionary image of the wild animal embedded in denial.
فَرَّتْ مِن قَسْوَرَةٍ supplies the fleeing motion that completes the animal analogy for turning away from the reminder.
The Torah-bearers are likened to a donkey carrying books and then called people who كَذَّبُوا۟ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ, joining an animal image, failed reception, and denial in one ayah.

The one who clings to earth and follows desire is likened to a panting dog, and the ayah identifies this as the likeness of those who كَذَّبُوا۟ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا; denial is again made perceptible as animal behavior.

When the staff appears as a snake, Moses وَلَّىٰ مُدْبِرًا وَلَمْ يُعَقِّبْ: he turns and runs without looking back, a precise bodily use of the root and a reversal of the wild animal that stops to look behind.
The second telling repeats that Moses وَلَّىٰ مُدْبِرًا وَلَمْ يُعَقِّبْ, confirming bodily flight without a backward turn as a distinct form of tawallī.
The believers climb away without turning toward anyone while the Messenger calls them from behind, combining bodily retreat, a voice left at their backs, and failure to respond.
Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it gives a direct nonlexical definition of the section's اِبْتِغَاء as desire joined to exertion.
وَٱبْتَغُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِ ٱلْوَسِيلَةَ is paired with striving in God's path, making seeking toward Him an active, effortful orientation.
The very beings invoked by others themselves يَبْتَغُونَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمُ ٱلْوَسِيلَةَ and compete in nearness, fixing both the sought direction and the exertion of approach.
Travelers heading for the Sacred House are described as يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلًا مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ وَرِضْوَٰنًا, so physical destination and the search for divine pleasure coincide.
Secret counsel becomes good when it orders charity, recognized good, or reconciliation and is done ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ, showing concrete deeds directed solely at divine approval.
The believers' claimed going out in God's path and ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِى is tested against secret affection for His enemies, making the sought approval govern the direction of loyalty.
The Messenger asks no payment except that whoever wills take a path to his Lord, joining absence of human recompense with a freely chosen Godward direction.
Whoever hopes to meet his Lord must act rightly and keep worship unmixed, so the anticipated encounter governs the purity of the seeker’s present direction.
Those who do good receive ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ and more, while gloom and humiliation do not cover their faces; the ayah brings the “best” denied in 92:9 into relation with the face sought in 92:20.
Righteousness is not merely أَن تُوَلُّوا۟ وُجُوهَكُمْ east or west; faith and generous action give bodily direction its moral content, a precise boundary on the section's face imagery.
The qiblah is made a test distinguishing one who follows the Messenger from one who يَنقَلِبُ عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيْهِ, turning back on his heels rather than accepting the new direction.
The People of the Book will not follow the Prophet's qiblah, nor he theirs, setting faithful face-direction against competing orientations and desire-led following.
فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّىٰ states the negative counterpart to 92's affirmation of the best and prepares the explicit كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ of 75:32.
The ayah explicitly opposes following رِضْوَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ to returning with God's سَخَط, exactly enacting the dictionary statement that رضى is the contrary of anger.
Those condemned اتَّبَعُوا۟ مَآ أَسْخَطَ ٱللَّهَ وَكَرِهُوا۟ رِضْوَٰنَهُ: their following has the wrong direction, and anger is set against the pleasure they reject.
God does not يَرْضَىٰ disbelief for His servants but is pleased with gratitude, placing denial and رضى on opposite sides of the same moral turn.
Monasticism was invented ٱبْتِغَآءَ رِضْوَٰنِ ٱللَّهِ but was not observed as it should have been; intended seeking is tested by whether effort remains faithful to its object.
فَكَذَّبَ وَعَصَىٰ gives Pharaoh's denial and disobedience, the stance whose bodily direction and strenuous movement appear in 79:22.
ثُمَّ أَدْبَرَ يَسْعَىٰ shows a man striving while headed away, the exact reversal of the section's tireless seeker whose face remains on the goal.
The question أَفَرَءَيْتَ ٱلَّذِى تَوَلَّىٰ introduces a turner whose interrupted giving is specified in the next ayah.
وَأَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ depicts giving a little and then stopping, reversing both the generous act and the persistent search developed in the section.
The blazing fire calls مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, making backward movement and turning away the very orientation that carries a person toward the threatened fire rather than the sought face.
The one called by the fire جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ, gathering and hoarding; this supplies the withholding practice paired with the turn in 70:17 and reverses Godward giving.
The Prophet is told to turn from one who تَوَلَّىٰ عَن ذِكْرِنَا and wants only worldly life; the object desired exposes why that person's face is directed away.
إِلَّا مَن تَوَلَّىٰ وَكَفَرَ identifies turning away and disbelief as the opposite stance to the satisfied faces earlier in the same surah.
Those who do not hope for meeting God are رَضُوا۟ بِٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا and remain heedless, contrasting satisfaction that settles into the near life with satisfaction reached by seeking the Lord.
أَرَضِيتُم بِٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا مِنَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ rebukes people who cling heavily to the earth instead of moving out, a wrong satisfaction that halts the required journey.
Whoever desires only the immediate world receives a measured portion and ends in Hell; beside 17:19 it shows how the sought object determines the direction and end of striving.
The phrase تَبْتَغِى مَرْضَاتَ أَزْوَٰجِكَ uses the same search-for-pleasure construction with human approval as its object, marking a boundary around seeking that overrides what God made lawful.
Charity spoiled by reminders, injury, and being seen by people reverses the unrecompensed, face-seeking gift: the outward act remains while its gaze is fixed on a human audience.
The ayah places وَٱبْتَغِ the Hereafter opposite وَلَا تَبْغِ corruption on earth, using the same root for two incompatible objects and making direction decisive.
Whoever يَبْتَغِ a religion other than submission will not have it accepted; effortful seeking does not save a search aimed away from the accepted direction.
وَوَجَدَكَ ضَآلًّا فَهَدَىٰ reverses the lost-animal illustration: here God finds one without the way and supplies guidance, making the seeker also one who has first been found.
Feeding the needy person, orphan, and captive despite love of the food supplies the concrete gift whose sole motive and refusal of repayment are voiced in 76:9.
كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ gives the universal passing-away against which the remaining face of the Lord in 55:27 becomes visible.
After passing the junction, Moses asks for food and names the journey's fatigue; this ayah registers the exertion and overshooting that lead to retracing their steps in 18:64.
The brothers' recognition “Are you indeed Joseph?” and Joseph's answer bring the search ordered in 12:87 to a face-to-face discovery.
God's question “What made you hasten from your people, Moses?” identifies the directed haste whose goal and desired رضى Moses states in 20:84.
Whoever hopes for the meeting with God is assured that God's appointed term is coming, supporting the section's movement from sustained seeking to encounter.
The humble are characterized by conviction that they will meet their Lord and return to Him, giving the faceward movement both an encounter and a return.
On the Day truthfulness benefits the truthful, رَّضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ makes satisfaction reciprocal between Lord and servants.
The first emigrants, helpers, and faithful followers reach the reciprocal end رَّضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ after a life of committed following.
Those whose faith withstands opposing loyalties receive gardens and the mutual verdict رَضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ, a communal form of the search's satisfying end.
The best creatures receive lasting gardens and reciprocal pleasure, and the ayah links that end to one who fears his Lord, clarifying whom the promised رضى belongs to.
After promised gardens and dwellings, وَرِضْوَٰنٌ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ makes God's approval the greater destination beyond the visible rewards.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord through the recurring turns of day and night لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضَىٰ, linking persevering orientation to eventual satisfaction.
The poor emigrants leave homes and wealth while يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلًا مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضْوَٰنًا, making costly physical displacement an enacted search for divine approval.
God guides those who follow His pleasure into paths of peace and out of darkness into light, turning رضوان into a followed direction rather than a static feeling.
The believers return with grace and no harm after وَٱتَّبَعُوا۟ رِضْوَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ; divine pleasure is something followed through fearful circumstances.
God guides إِلَيْهِ مَنْ أَنَابَ, so turning back to Him becomes the motion by which guidance acquires a direction.
God chooses whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back, again expressing guidance as a Godward reorientation.
وَأَنِيبُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ وَأَسْلِمُوا۟ لَهُ commands a turn toward the Lord before punishment arrives, the positive reversal of tawallī as departure.
Abraham says إِنِّى ذَاهِبٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّى سَيَهْدِينِ, making physical departure an image of going toward the Lord under His guidance.
فَفِرُّوٓا۟ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ gives flight a destination in God, reversing the fleeing animal whose movement is defined only by what it leaves behind.
Lot's household is told to travel by night and let no one look back; the forbidden backward gaze gives a concrete boundary to the section's animal that stops and looks behind.
The repeated command that Lot's family depart at night and not let anyone look back keeps rescue dependent on an undivided forward direction.
Believers meeting an advancing force are forbidden to تُوَلُّوهُمُ ٱلْأَدْبَارَ, a literal bodily turning of backs with moral consequence.
The ayah defines the narrow tactical exceptions to turning one's back in battle and otherwise ties that bodily turn to divine anger.
At Hunayn the believers' numbers do not avail them and they وَلَّيْتُم مُّدْبِرِينَ, a concrete collective scene of bodies turning back under pressure.
Those who had covenanted not to يُوَلُّونَ ٱلْأَدْبَٰرَ show how a bodily turn of the back can also violate an inward commitment.
فَتَوَلَّىٰ فِرْعَوْنُ فَجَمَعَ كَيْدَهُۥ ثُمَّ أَتَىٰ shows Pharaoh depart, gather his plan, and return, a clear bodily-departure sense of tawallī directed to a hostile purpose.
Pharaoh فَتَوَلَّىٰ بِرُكْنِهِ and dismisses Moses as magician or madman, joining a posture of turning with verbal refusal of the message.
عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ stages tawallī as an interpersonal bodily turn, with the next ayah identifying the person from whom the face was turned.
أَن جَآءَهُ ٱلْأَعْمَىٰ gives the arrival of the blind man as the occasion of the turn in 80:1 and makes the bodily movement morally legible.
The command فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ shows that turning away can also be a divinely commanded withdrawal from entrenched deniers, a boundary on treating every bodily turn as blameworthy.
The person reminded of God's signs then turns away and forgets what his hands sent ahead; coverings over hearts and heaviness in ears spell out the refusal to hear within that turn.
The wrongdoer is one reminded of his Lord's signs who ثُمَّ أَعْرَضَ عَنْهَا, a concise nonbodily turn away from received instruction.
When favored, the human being turns away and distances himself by his side; bodily posture expresses inward refusal, while distress reverses his mood into despair.
The same repeated image—turning away and distancing by one's side after blessing—shows how a body's orientation can disclose a settled stance.
Obeying the Messenger is obedience to God, while مَن تَوَلَّىٰ marks rejection of that obedience; the Messenger is not appointed as their keeper.
Obedience to God and the Messenger is commanded, and فَإِن تَوَلَّيْتُمْ leaves the Messenger responsible only for clear delivery, again defining the turn as refused command.
The same obedience formula ends with فَإِن تَوَلَّيْتُمْ and the Messenger's duty of clear conveyance, a repeated nonbodily use of turning away.
When summoned to God and His messenger for judgment, a group becomes مُعْرِضُونَ, supplying the actual call they refuse after the turn named in 24:47.
The man given God's signs slips out of them and is pursued by Satan; this withdrawal prepares the dog image and denial named in 7:176.
Disbelievers are likened to animals hearing only a caller's cry and sound, a herd scene that makes failure to listen and understand perceptible.
Those who neither hear nor reason are likened to livestock and said to be further astray in path, joining animal behavior, failed hearing, and lost direction.
People with ears that do not hear and eyes that do not see are likened to livestock and called heedless, expanding the section's turn-by-nonlistening into an animal analogy.
The prohibition against turning one's cheek from people uses literal face posture to expose pride, a human-scale boundary on how bodily orientation carries moral meaning.
وَعَنَتِ ٱلْوُجُوهُ لِلْحَىِّ ٱلْقَيُّومِ lets “faces” stand for whole persons humbled before the living, sustaining Lord.
Noah asks his people for no wealth, says his reward is only with God, and refuses to drive away those who will meet their Lord, combining no human payment with the awaited encounter.
The command to follow messengers who ask no payment and are rightly guided joins freedom from worldly recompense to a trustworthy direction.

وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ may mean not to give expecting an increase; on that reading it is a specific boundary against the return-seeking gift opposed by 92:19-20, though the wording also permits other readings.

The brothers expect يَخْلُ لَكُمْ وَجْهُ أَبِيكُمْ after removing Joseph; if “your father's face” denotes his undivided regard, it is a human and morally distorted analogue to seeking a face as the person’s attention.
